body.text: Beijing Scan is ORF’s monthly insight on China, analysing crucial political, economic, foreign policy, and military developments.
Figure 1: Key Takeaways of China’s Economy in October

China recorded a trade surplus of US$105.28 billion in October 2026, taking its cumulative surplus for January–October to US$1.043 trillion. China is on course to surpass its 2025 record of US$1.2 trillion—reached in November last year—potentially a month earlier. October exports grew 35.2 percent year-on-year, driven by strong global demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related hardware, including semiconductors, data-centre servers and networking equipment, as well as automobiles and electric vehicles.
Figure 2: China’s Trade Surplus: 2021-October 2026

The export surge reflects China’s expanding role in global technology supply chains and its reliance on overseas markets to absorb industrial overcapacity amid weak domestic consumption. Imports also grew 41.6 percent in October, supported by demand for semiconductors and data-centre components. The widening surplus may intensify trade friction, particularly with the European Union, whose trade deficit with China reached US$310.7 billion in January–October.

China’s GDP grew 4.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, recovering from a multi-year low of 4.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Growth averaged 4.6 percent over the first nine months, bringing it back within Beijing’s 4.5–5 percent annual target. Industrial production, up 5.5 percent, led the charge, driven by stronger factory output, export-oriented manufacturing and demand for AI-related hardware, alongside targeted fiscal support. Retail sales, however, rose only 1.1 percent, while weak household consumption and sluggish property investment continued to constrain the broader recovery.

Meanwhile, China’s producer-price inflation (PPI) accelerated to 5.7 percent in October, its highest since June 2022, up from 5 percent in September. Factory-gate prices have also risen, reversing nearly three years of deflation. The PPI pressure, however, has not translated into consumer inflation, with the consumer price index (CPI) slowing to 0.7 percent from 0.9 percent and core inflation falling to 0.8 percent, its lowest in 2026.
Figure 3: China’s Producer Price Inflation (2020-26)
Source: Author's calculations based on NBS and monthly year-on-year changes in China's PPI

The divergence underscores the uneven nature of the price recovery. Nine industries, led by coal mining, oil and gas extraction, and fuel processing, contributed over six percentage points to the rise in producer prices. Nevertheless, only 15 of the 30 major industrial sectors recorded price increases, mostly in upstream and energy-intensive sectors. Multiple downstream industries, including automobiles, pharmaceuticals, and general-purpose machinery, remained in deflation. October’s figures point to rising producer prices driven by higher input costs, rather than a broad-based economic recovery. China’s factories face mounting costs, but demand remains weak.

China has transformed its chemicals industry into a global powerhouse, expanding capacity 18-fold over 25 years to control over 45 percent of global capacity in basic chemicals and plastic resins. Since 2020, China’s ethylene, polyethylene and polypropylene production capacity has surged by 80, 75 and 71 percent, respectively.
Figure 4: China’s Dominance in Chemicals
Source: Rhodium Group research

Decades of state support—subsidies, tax concessions, cheap financing and industrial parks—have pushed chemical production capacity beyond domestic demand, leaving nearly a third of Chinese chemical producers loss-making. The resulting pressure to export is driving capacity closures in Europe and Northeast Asia, fuelling calls for trade barriers and a broader industrial-policy backlash. In India, China’s share of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) imports surged from 3 percent in 2020 to 45 percent in 2025.

The Communist Party of China’s (CPC) 20th Central Committee convened its Fifth Plenum in October, placing anti-corruption and internal discipline at the centre of its deliberations. The Plenum reviewed 34 disciplinary cases, expelled 33 senior officials from the Party and removed one official from his Party post. The military accounted for 16 of those expelled, underscoring the scale of the ongoing purge within the People's Liberation Army (PLA). Among those expelled were prominent figures such as Zhang Youxia, former senior vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC), and Ma Xingrui, former Party secretary of Xinjiang.
Figure 5: The Key Takeaways of the Fifth Plenum
Source: Author-generated based on Plenum Documents

The Plenum also sought to institutionalise the Party’s emphasis on internal discipline. It adopted the ‘Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance’. Although Xi Jinping has consistently prioritised anti-corruption and internal discipline, the resolution seeks to move these efforts beyond periodic disciplinary campaigns by establishing a more systematic framework for Party oversight, cadre management and accountability. Both the mass expulsions and the resolution reflect Xi’s determination to tighten political control over the Party and its institutions. The scale of the purges, however, also exposes the depth of the corruption and disciplinary problems within the Party’s ranks.

In an explainer, Xi argued that the growing share of younger cadres, born after Deng Xiaoping’s Reform and Opening Up, is a concern for the CPC. He urged these cadres to strengthen ideological commitment and organisational discipline to safeguard the Party’s long-term rule, a message that reflects Xi’s shift towards prioritising national security over development. Another report on Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building presents ‘rigorous Party self-governance’, enforced through anti-corruption campaigns, as essential to maintaining internal discipline and addressing public discontent.

This emphasis reinforces the narrative the CPC advanced during its 105th anniversary in 2026: the claimed superiority of its governance model. Xi has credited the Party’s centralised, one-party system with delivering economic growth, social stability and modernisation. The principle of “unified leadership”, with Xi at its core, underpins this claim by enabling long-term planning, resource mobilisation and consistent policy implementation.

The Fifth Plenum’s adoption of the resolution on Party self-governance takes on particular significance ahead of the 21st Party Congress in 2027, when Xi is widely expected to secure another term. It signals that the anti-corruption campaign will remain central to his agenda, extending beyond individual purges to strengthen the Party’s organisational foundations and ensure political continuity.

China and Pakistan conducted their first joint army exercise with regular army formations, named Karakoram-2026, from 14 to 22 October 2026 at Korla in China’s Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. The exercise marked a notable expansion of bilateral military cooperation beyond specialised counterterrorism and special forces training. What distinguished it was its focus on the use of regular army formations, combined-arms capabilities, mixed-unit operations and joint command procedures.
Image 1: Sino-Pakistan Karakorum 2026
Source: CCTV 7

This reinforced push to strengthen tactical and operational interoperability—enabling army personnel to develop common procedures, communicate effectively and coordinate operations within a shared command framework—represents an important step in Sino-Pakistan bilateral defence cooperation. Rising interoperability, coupled with the expansion of joint military exercises into conventional ground combat operations, sends a strong strategic signal to India.

Chinese military experts also anticipate deeper intelligence sharing and joint operational collaboration to build military trust. High-altitude training addresses challenges posed by thin air, difficult terrain, degraded communications and logistical constraints across the China–Pakistan border, where elevations exceed 5,000 metres. These capabilities could also prove relevant against India, their common adversary.

The US Space Force’s acceptance of the Meadowlands electromagnetic warfare system for operational use, expanding its ground-based capability to disrupt adversary satellite communications, has triggered the PLA’s threat perceptions of low Earth orbit (LEO) constellations as an emerging battlespace.
Image 2: US Space Force’s Meadowlands Counter-Space System
Source: Defense News

On 19 October, the PLA Daily published three articles on this theme. The first article argued that low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are transforming modern warfare by integrating communications, reconnaissance, unmanned platforms and precision strikes into faster, decentralised kill networks. Drawing on the Russia–Ukraine conflict, it highlighted growing countermeasures, including electronic jamming, anti-satellite weapons, directed energy and cyberattacks. It also identified AI-driven electronic warfare, resilient satellite networks and ground infrastructure protection as emerging priorities, while warning that intensifying competition threatens global space governance.

The second article argued that targeting ground infrastructure offers a more practical and cost-effective way to neutralise LEO satellite constellations than destroying satellites in orbit. Ground stations, control centres and launch facilities remain vulnerable bottlenecks. It urged military planners to prioritise attacks on these nodes while strengthening their protection through redundancy, reinforced facilities and coordinated space-ground defence.

The third article examined how the US was developing an integrated anti-satellite warfare capability. It highlighted the commissioning of the Meadowlands electronic jamming system and the Bounty Hunter surveillance system, alongside orbital and kinetic capabilities. The authors argued that Washington was moving from technological experimentation towards operational deployment, integrating detection, electronic warfare, satellite interception and allied networks to secure space superiority, thereby degrading China’s access to space-based assets during a contingency.
Figure 6: China’s Emerging Opinion on LEO Constellations
Source: Author-generated based on three PLA Daily articles

These three articles provide a glimpse into China’s evolving thinking on space warfare. The debate centres on three interconnected priorities: exploiting LEO constellations to strengthen joint operational capabilities, denying adversaries similar advantages, and protecting China’s own space-based infrastructure in an increasingly contested environment. The first two articles, written by experts from China’s Space Engineering University, are particularly noteworthy. They shed light on the institutional thinking shaping the PLA’s emerging approach to space warfare.

During the final sea trials of the Type-76 amphibious assault ship Sichuan, China’s first shipborne stealth reconnaissance-strike drone, the GJ-21, completed its maiden take-off and landing operations on 30 October. Sichuan, with a full-load displacement of over 40,000 tons, is equipped with an automated landing guidance system, an integrated electric power system, and electromagnetic catapult and arrestor technologies, enabling it to serve as both a versatile amphibious assault ship and a mothership for drone operations. The recent launch is the first publicly reported catapult launch and arrested recovery of a jet combat drone from an amphibious assault ship.
Image 3: GJ-21 Take-off from Type 76 Sichuan Warship
Source: Author AI-assisted creation

Gongji-21 (GJ-21; 攻击-21, meaning ‘Attack-21’), a naval variant of the GJ-11 stealth attack drone, is a jet-powered, tailless flying-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) developed by Hongdu Aviation Industry Group (AVIC). Operating from the Sichuan amphibious assault ship, it could extend the PLA Navy’s operational reach, conduct high-risk missions in defended airspace and enhance distributed naval aviation and long-range strike capabilities. A potential two-tonne internal payload would strengthen China’s next-generation combat-air system.

Authored by Atul Kumar and Kalpit A. Mankikar, Fellows, and Srijan Shukla, Associate Fellow, at the Strategic Studies Programme, together with Shruti Mishra, Research Intern, Observer Research Foundation (ORF). The views expressed are those of the authors.
